extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and practitioners of literary criticism and liberal education (educators, critics, and educated public interested in humanities vs. science debate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for literary criticism and for choosing the place of humane letters in education — assessing how literature, poetry, and art relate knowledge to conduct and beauty and how critics should judge literature's historical currents and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of dealing with facts (value of natural science)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of nature trains the habit of dealing with facts by constant appeal to observation and experiment; this discipline is 'a most valuable discipline' and every one should have some experience of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science's insistence on observable demonstration (e.g., showing that wax converts to carbonic acid and water) provides an indispensable discipline; include empirical training in education but recognize its limits when applied exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the constitution of human nature (four powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nature is built up by the powers of conduct, intellect and knowledge, beauty, and social life and manners; education must take into account this constitution and adjust the claims of these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing curricula or judging educational aims, ensure balance among moral/conduct formation, intellectual knowledge, aesthetic cultivation, and social manners; neglect of any yields incompleteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relating knowledge to conduct and to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a pervasive human instinct to relate pieces of knowledge to our sense for conduct and to our sense for beauty; humane letters satisfy this desire and are therefore essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works and curricula by their capacity to connect abstract or factual knowledge with ethical and aesthetic concerns — does the work help readers integrate facts into moral/aesthetic life?

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish instrument-knowledges from educative knowledges
rubrics_metrics.description: Some knowledges are instrumental (specialist tools) and may not directly serve the instinct for beauty or conduct; the generality of men should not be educated solely in instrument-knowledges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an education program or the aims of a work, ask whether it is primarily a technical instrument for specialists or whether it cultivates broader humane capacities; a little mathematics or technical training suffices for many, but not as the whole education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanities as mediators between science and the instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science supplies knowledge but rarely relates that knowledge to the instincts for conduct and beauty; humane letters (poetry, eloquence, art) have the power to perform this mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value literature and art for their capacity to translate modern scientific conceptions into forms that engage the moral and aesthetic sensibilities; judge works partly on how successfully they perform this integrative task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of poetry and eloquence to engage emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and eloquence have, for the vast majority of men, the power of calling out the emotions and thereby influencing their sense for conduct and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literary works by their experiential, emotional effect on readers: do they move, refresh, fortify, elevate, or quicken moral and aesthetic feeling? Use readers' experience as evidence of efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience as the test of humane letters' effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether poetry and eloquence exercise the power to affect conduct and beauty is to be judged by experience; the appeal is empirical (from experience of readers' responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and educators should look to historical and present experience of how works have moved people rather than abstract theory alone; provide examples and testimonies where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of ancient/artistic criticism of life
rubrics_metrics.description: The art, poetry, and eloquence of antiquity (even with erroneous natural knowledge) have a fortifying and suggestive power capable of helping to relate modern scientific results to human needs for conduct and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating canonical or older works, consider their enduring capacity to frame life and support moral/aesthetic reflection despite outdated factual beliefs; don't dismiss them simply for historical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invidious comparison; humanities complement science
rubrics_metrics.description: One should avoid harsh comparisons between humane letters and natural sciences; humanities do different but complementary work, and students of letters will still learn major scientific conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or curricular judgments should recognize complementarity rather than seeking a winner — a balanced curriculum acknowledges that science forces conceptions on all, while letters relate them to human instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational recommendation for majority: prioritize humane letters
rubrics_metrics.description: For the majority of mankind (those without exceptional aptitudes for natural science), it is better to be educated in humane letters than to concentrate wholly on natural science, because letters call out human being at more points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding broad curricula for non-specialists, favor courses that cultivate moral and aesthetic capacities even while including some scientific literacy; prioritize what engages most learners deeply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical (Greek) literature as an unrivaled service to the instinct for beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the instinct for beauty is especially served by Greek literature and art, then Greek should be retained in education because it uniquely fosters the sense for symmetry and high combining of details into a supreme total effect (symmetria prisca).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating the place of classical languages in curricula, consider Greek's unique contributions to aesthetic formation (e.g., symmetry in architecture and art); curricular defenders may argue for Greek on aesthetic grounds rather than mere antiquarianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain the master-current of an epoch's literature
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the critic's highest functions is to identify the master-current in an epoch's literature and distinguish it from minor currents; this shows justness of spirit in criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should map major streams vs. minor trends, explain which will most influence the future, and avoid conflating interesting minor schools with the central current; support claims with historical and textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justness of spirit as indispensable critical quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Justness of spirit — fairness, accurate judgment — is an indispensable quality for a critic; lacking it, a critic may misidentify central tendencies (as Carlyle is said to have done).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate critics and critical judgments by whether they exhibit fairness and proportion; beware of excessive self-will, eccentricity, or partisan distortions when appraising critical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic method: work from within outwards (originality and individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must work 'from within outwards' — originality arises from expressing individuality; this method is central to genuine poetic creation and liberation from routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging literary works, favor those showing authentic individuality and inner necessity rather than mere adherence to external conventions; assess whether the work reveals an original inward life expressed outwardly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's reforming role: dissolve old systems without acrimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern criticism must act as a dissolvent of obsolete inherited systems of ideas and institutions, but should avoid becoming an 'acrid dissolvent' — i.e., reform should be discerning and constructive, not merely destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In critical judgment, combine transformative insight with measured appraisal; aim to show how literature helps modernize thought without gratuitous destructiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying and combating philistinism
rubrics_metrics.description: A central object of modern critical engagement (as exemplified by Heine) is opposition to philistinism — the narrow, respectable commonplace that stifles culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works partly by whether they resist or expose philistinism; a critic's task includes diagnosing cultural philistinism and defending higher standards of taste and intellectual courage.
